subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Cognitive processing (models of memory, schema theory)
Reliability of cognitive processes (reconstructive memory, biases)
Cognitive processing in the digital world (HL)
Ethical considerations and research methods in the cognitive approach

questions.q: The multi-store model of memory (Atkinson and Shiffrin) distinguishes between:
options: Sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory
The phonological loop and the sketchpad
questions.explain: The multi-store model proposes three structurally separate stores with information passing between them via attention and rehearsal.

questions.q: The working memory model (Baddeley and Hitch) improved on the multi-store model by proposing that short-term memory is:
options: An active system of several components rather than a single store
questions.explain: Working memory replaced the unitary STM with a central executive coordinating the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad (later the episodic buffer).

questions.q: In the working memory model, verbal and acoustic information is handled by the:
questions.explain: The phonological loop stores and rehearses speech-based information, while the visuospatial sketchpad handles visual and spatial material.

questions.q: Bartlett's 'War of the Ghosts' study found that participants distorted the story towards their own cultural expectations on repeated recall. This supports:
questions.explain: Recall was reconstructive: pre-existing schemas shaped what was remembered, causing systematic distortions.

questions.q: Brewer and Treyens found participants often 'recalled' books in an academic office that contained none. The best explanation is that:
options: Their schema for an office reconstructed the memory
Books were shown on a screen
questions.explain: Schema-consistent items (books) were falsely recalled, showing schemas guide reconstruction and can introduce errors.

questions.q: Loftus and Palmer (1974) altered the verb (e.g. 'smashed' vs 'hit') in a question about a filmed car crash and found it changed speed estimates. This demonstrates:
options: The effect of leading questions on reconstructive memory
That memory is a perfect recording
The role of the phonological loop
questions.explain: The wording of a post-event question influenced recall, evidence that memory is reconstructive and open to distortion.

questions.q: The misinformation effect refers to:
options: Post-event information distorting a person's memory of the original event
Forgetting due to lack of rehearsal
questions.explain: Exposure to misleading information after an event can alter what is later recalled about it.

questions.q: Loftus and Pickrell's 'lost in the shopping mall' procedure is most often cited as evidence that:
options: Entirely false memories can be implanted through suggestion
Emotion has no effect on memory
questions.explain: Some participants came to 'remember' a fabricated childhood event, showing suggestion can create false memories.

questions.q: Confirmation bias is the tendency to:
options: Search for and interpret information in a way that supports existing beliefs
Remember the first item in a list best
Rely on the most recent information
questions.explain: Confirmation bias leads people to favour evidence that fits their prior beliefs and discount evidence that does not.

questions.q: A cognitive bias in which an initial reference value unduly influences a later numerical judgement is called:
questions.explain: Anchoring occurs when an initial value (the anchor) biases subsequent estimates towards it.

questions.q: A flashbulb memory (Brown and Kulik) is a vivid and detailed memory of:
options: The moment one learned of a surprising, emotionally significant event
A procedural skill such as cycling
The layout of a familiar room
questions.explain: Flashbulb memories are highly detailed recollections of the circumstances in which shocking news was received.

questions.q: Neisser and Harsch's study of memories for the Challenger disaster is important because it showed that flashbulb memories:
options: Can be inaccurate even when people are highly confident
questions.explain: Reports changed substantially over time despite high confidence, challenging the idea that flashbulb memories are especially accurate.

questions.q: Lazarus's appraisal theory proposes that an emotional response depends primarily on:
options: The person's cognitive appraisal of the situation
questions.explain: Appraisal theory holds that how an event is cognitively interpreted determines the emotion experienced.

questions.q: A person is extremely confident about exactly where they were when they heard major news, but independent records show several details are wrong. This best illustrates that:
options: Confidence in emotional memories does not guarantee accuracy
questions.explain: As in Neisser and Harsch, high confidence can coexist with real inaccuracy in emotionally charged memories.

questions.q: Which brain structure is most strongly implicated in the emotional enhancement of memory?
questions.explain: The amygdala modulates the consolidation of emotionally arousing memories, often via stress hormones.

questions.q: Sparrow et al. (2011), studying the 'Google effect', found people were less likely to remember information when they believed it:
options: Had been saved and would remain accessible on a computer
Was presented first in a list
questions.explain: When people expect to be able to look something up later, they remember where to find it rather than the information itself (transactive memory).

questions.q: Transactive memory in the digital age refers to:
options: Relying on external sources or devices to store and retrieve information
A component of the working memory model
questions.explain: People offload storage and retrieval onto external systems (including devices and other people), remembering how to access information.

questions.q: A study reports that heavy media multitaskers score lower on an attention-filtering task. A methodologically sound caution is that:
options: The correlation does not establish that multitasking causes poorer filtering
The result proves technology improves memory
questions.explain: Such findings are typically correlational; pre-existing differences could explain both the multitasking and the attention scores.

questions.q: A general limitation of research on cognition in the digital world is that:
options: Much of it is correlational and technologies change rapidly, limiting firm conclusions
It is always experimental with random assignment
questions.explain: Fast-moving technology and reliance on correlational designs make robust causal conclusions difficult in this emerging area.

questions.q: A strength of laboratory experiments in cognitive psychology is high control over variables, but a frequent weakness is:
options: The absence of any independent variable
questions.explain: Tight control aids internal validity, but artificial tasks and settings may not reflect memory or thinking in everyday life.

questions.q: Demand characteristics occur when participants:
options: Guess the aim of the study and adjust their behaviour
questions.explain: Cues in a study can lead participants to infer its purpose and respond accordingly, threatening validity.

questions.q: Implanting false memories, as in false-memory research, raises particular ethical concerns about:
options: Deception and potential psychological harm, requiring careful debriefing
questions.explain: Creating false memories involves deception and possible distress, so thorough debriefing and safeguards are essential.

questions.q: To reduce demand characteristics in a memory experiment, a researcher could most appropriately:
options: Use a cover story so participants do not know the true aim, then debrief them
Tell participants exactly what result is expected
Let participants choose their own condition
questions.explain: A mild cover story reduces participants tailoring responses to the aim; a full debrief then addresses the ethics of the deception.

questions.q: Because memory is reconstructive, cognitive research implies that eyewitness testimony should be treated as:
options: Potentially unreliable and open to distortion
questions.explain: Leading questions, misinformation and schemas can all distort eyewitness accounts, so testimony must be interpreted with caution.
